meta.title: Who really said "Bigamy Is Having One Spouse Too Many. Monogamy Is the Same"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Erica Jong. She printed it in Fear of Flying (1973) credited to "Anonymous (a woman)." The joke was already in print in 1922.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Bigamy Is Having One Spouse Too Many. Monogamy Is the Same'?
meta.ogDescription: Erica Jong quoted it as an epigraph and signed it "Anonymous (a woman)." The joke is traceable to 1922 — and a precursor to 1841.

answer.label: Not Erica Jong — an anonymous joke she quoted
answer.authorDates: Author unidentified · in print by 1922, still unsigned in 1942
answer.sourceLine: Erica Jong did print this joke — as the epigraph to chapter one of Fear of Flying (1973) — but she signed it “—Anonymous (a woman),” not with her own name. Quote Investigator traces the gag back through anonymous printings to an 1841 precursor and finds no single originator ↗. One further wrinkle: every dated printing in that record says “wife” or “husband” — the tidy gender-neutral “spouse” version is a later smoothing, and is in fact the headline Quote Investigator wrote for its own article.

source.heading: Where the joke actually shows up in print

docMeta.dd: Robert Webster Jones, 1922 — Dorrance & Company, Philadelphia
Chapter I, “Bluebeard Tells Why He Killed Wives,” page 18
Erica Jong, Fear of Flying (1973) — where the epigraph is credited to “Anonymous (a woman)”

source.excerpt: I could go on all night telling you about my other wives and the causes of their sudden shufflings-off … The proverb says, ‘A word to the wives is sufficient,’ but I never found it so. Not by a long shot. I found action more effective than words. They say bigamy means one wife too many; but so does monogamy sometimes.
trail: 1922 — Robert Webster Jones gives the first recorded “bigamy…monogamy” pairing to the ghost of Bluebeard: “They say bigamy means one wife too many; but so does monogamy sometimes.” Confirmed on page 18 of the scanned 1922 edition ↗.

1929 — The Literary Digest prints a far closer form, crediting the British magazine London Opinion rather than a person: “Bigamy is having one wife too many. Monogamy, in certain instances, is the same thing.” Cited by Quote Investigator to the issue of 22 June 1929 ↗.

1942 — H. L. Mencken includes the saying in his New Dictionary of Quotations without naming an originator, and The Reader’s Digest reprints it that September as “Author unidentified.” Both printings are documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
1973 — Erica Jong opens chapter one with the “husband” wording, signed “—Anonymous (a woman).” Fear of Flying was published that year by Holt, Rinehart and Winston ↗.
source.excerptNote: Spoken by the shade of Bluebeard in a comic mock-interview. This is the earliest printing Quote Investigator documents that pairs “bigamy” and “monogamy” — the wording is not yet the modern one, and it carries no author’s name beyond Jones, who is writing in Bluebeard’s voice.
source.rightsNote: No status is asserted for the wording on this page: it is an anonymous joke with no identified author and no identifiable first publication, and the “spouse” form in particular matches no dated printing on record. The 1922 and 1929 printings quoted above were published before 1931 and are out of copyright in the United States. Erica Jong’s Fear of Flying (1973) is in copyright, but the epigraph she reproduced there was already circulating unsigned, and she credited it as anonymous rather than claiming it.

author.name: Erica Jong
author.heading: Erica Jong quoted it — and said so
author.metaLine: Born 26 March 1942 · American novelist, poet and satirist
author.bio: Erica Mann Jong is an American novelist, satirist, poet and teacher, born in New York City on 26 March 1942. Her 1973 debut Fear of Flying was famously controversial for its frank treatment of female sexual desire, figured prominently in second-wave feminism, and has sold tens of millions of copies. She opened its first chapter with this joke as an epigraph — and credited it to “Anonymous (a woman),” which is precisely the line the internet later deleted in order to hand her the credit.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This joke has been pinned on three different people across a century of reprinting. The paper trail supports none of them — and one of the three said so herself, in print, at the time.

items.why: Jong used the “husband” wording as the epigraph to chapter one of Fear of Flying in 1973 and signed it “—Anonymous (a woman).” Quote Investigator notes that she did not credit herself, indicating the joke was already in circulation ↗. Aggregators then dropped that byline and substituted hers — one such page credits it to Erica Jong flatly, with no source at all ↗.

The Wilde ascription surfaces in A Treasury of Humorous Quotations (1969), long after the joke was in print anonymously. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Wilde wrote or said it ↗, and the line does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Wilde page ↗.

Mencken printed the saying in his 1942 New Dictionary of Quotations without naming an originator, and The Reader’s Digest reprinted it that September marked “Author unidentified.” By 1970 an Omaha newspaper was crediting the line to Mencken himself. Quote Investigator documents each of those steps ↗.

No dated printing on record uses “spouse.” The citations run “wife” (1922, 1929, 1942, 1969, 1970) and “husband” (1973). The gender-neutral form is in fact the title Quote Investigator gave its own article ↗ — a researcher’s summary heading, not a historical quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is older and duller than any of the three names: an anonymous joke that mutated in print for well over a century, and the one person who could plausibly have claimed it — Erica Jong — explicitly refused to. Quote Investigator’s chronology runs from 1841 to 1973 without ever finding an author ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Erica Jong
lead: An epigraph is a strange piece of typography. It sits at the top of a chapter in the author’s book, set in the author’s typeface, and it is the one thing on the page the author did not write. Jong made that explicit — the line under her epigraph reads “—Anonymous (a woman).” But quotation databases scrape the quote and the nearest name, and the nearest name on that page is hers.

The same mechanism had already run twice on the same joke. H. L. Mencken put it in his 1942 dictionary with no originator named, and The Reader’s Digest reprinted it that September as “Author unidentified”; within a generation an Omaha newspaper was crediting the line to Mencken. A 1969 humour anthology handed it to Oscar Wilde, who is the default owner of any epigram nobody can place. Jong is simply the third and most durable name to be attached to a joke that has been signing itself ‘anonymous’ since before she was born.
context.detailsSummary: How old is the joke, really?
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology starts in 1841, with a Greenwich pensioner in a London character sketch who holds “that every man takes one wife too many whenever he is such a fool as to marry the first.” The words ‘bigamy’ and ‘monogamy’ are not there yet, but the shape of the joke is.

The first printing to use both words is the 1922 mock-interview book Light Interviews with Shades, where the ghost of Bluebeard delivers it: “They say bigamy means one wife too many; but so does monogamy sometimes.” Seven years later The Literary Digest ran a version very close to the modern one, crediting the British humour magazine London Opinion rather than any writer — which is how this joke has travelled for its entire documented life.
context.pull: She signed it “Anonymous (a woman).” The internet crossed that out and wrote her name.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the quip evolved over decades from anonymous antecedents (precursor 1841), that Erica Jong used the "husband" version as the chapter-one epigraph of Fear of Flying in 1973 credited to "Anonymous (a woman)", that there is no substantive evidence Oscar Wilde wrote or said it (first Wilde credit 1969), and that H. L. Mencken printed it in 1942 without specifying an originator. Also documents 1922 Light Interviews with Shades, 1929 Literary Digest ("Monogamy, in certain instances, is the same thing.—London Opinion"), Sept 1942 Reader's Digest "Author unidentified", and a 1970 Omaha World Herald credit to Mencken. The page's own title uses the word "Spouse".

The 1922 book Light Interviews with Shades by Robert Webster Jones (Philadelphia: Dorrance, 1922) contains, on page 18 in Chapter I "Bluebeard Tells Why He Killed Wives", the sentence: "They say bigamy means one wife too many; but so does monogamy sometimes." — verified in the scanned full text.

Wikiquote's Erica Jong page does not contain "Bigamy is having one husband too many. Monogamy is the same." in any section; it gives her birth date as 26 March 1942 and describes her as an American author and educator best known for Fear of Flying (1973).
Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page does not contain the bigamy/monogamy line in any section, including Misattributed.

Fear of Flying is a 1973 novel by Erica Jong, published by Holt, Rinehart and Winston in the United States. (The Wikipedia article does not reproduce the epigraph; the epigraph is documented by Quote Investigator, verified on paper.)

Erica Mann Jong, born March 26, 1942, is an American novelist, satirist, poet and teacher; her 1973 debut novel Fear of Flying was controversial for its attitudes towards female sexuality and figured prominently in second-wave feminism.

This aggregator page presents "Bigamy is having one husband too many. Monogamy is the same." attributed simply to Erica Jong, with no source or citation given — an example of the bare-attribution pattern.
